extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and established fiction writers seeking to build an author brand / market their work
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for fiction writers on identifying, articulating, and marketing a recognizable author brand so readers follow the author (not just a series), including how to discover brand elements, pitch them, and expand across genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a recognizable identity (brand) for you and your works
rubrics_metrics.description: Branding, in marketing terms for writers, is the process of establishing a recognizable identity—a brand— for you and your works in the marketplace of readers, and people who buy things for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your brand should operate in the marketplace: be identifiable to readers and gatekeepers (editors, agents, retailers). Think about what your brand needs to do for you and how to get it to do that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the fans follow your writing, not the series
rubrics_metrics.description: Build your author brand so that fans read whatever you write rather than only one series; aim to be known as the writer rather than known only for a single property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Neil Gaiman and N. K. Jemisin draw readers to the author across different works; some YA authors get 'locked into' a series and struggle to attract readers to other books. Craft branding that translates across projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what you do really well that makes you stand out
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide what you do that is distinctive and make that a central feature of your brand (e.g., magic systems, voice, characterization style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at your own output and other authors' careers to pick a memorable, repeatable element (Brandon: 'the magic system guy'; Jemisin: marrying literary techniques to fantasy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being locked into a series; plan for career flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Be deliberate so you don't accidentally let a series become the only thing people associate with you, which can make future non-series work fail commercially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe YA blockbuster dynamics where audiences focus on series. If you want breadth, craft your brand to encompass elements beyond a single series and signal that to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use feedback from friends, alpha readers, and beta readers to discover your brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask people who read your work to list what stands out about your writing; use recurring themes in their responses to identify brand elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework: Have multiple readers write down the things that stand out. Compare lists to find consistent connections and themes you may not see in yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate the highlights of your work into concise pitches
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn the distinctive elements of your writing into short, repeatable pitches so fans and gatekeepers can describe your books easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop three-sentence pitches for each new project that emphasize your brand elements so readers and fans can spread consistent messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use panels and conventions to test and refine brand messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Public appearances (panels, talks) reveal how people place you and give opportunities to hone how you talk about your brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note which panel topics you're repeatedly asked to speak on; ask for panels that align with your brand and practice messaging in public settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that the articulated brand may differ from the subconscious message readers internalize
rubrics_metrics.description: The way you describe your brand (articulation) is not necessarily the message readers will internalize about you; both levels matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about what you say publicly, but also recognize how repeated signals (tone, themes, recurring elements) create subconscious associations (Howard's example: 'that's the guy I buy all his books from').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick which aspects of public perception to lean into or push back against
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all perceptions are under your control; decide what external assumptions you want to embrace and which you want to counteract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: demographic or identity-based assumptions may affect how readers see your work. You can choose to emphasize or resist certain readings of your identity in relation to your brand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your brand need not represent the whole soul of your writing
rubrics_metrics.description: A brand can be a selected highlight or hallmark of your work rather than a complete statement of artistic intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may prefer to be known for many things (e.g., great characters) but deliberately foreground one memorable element (e.g., magic systems) because marketing and audience cognition favor distinct, repeatable signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attracting the wrong audience; ensure audience fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't position your brand so it draws readers who dislike your core strengths, because negative associations can harm future sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your articulated brand says something that repels a segment, those readers who encounter your work and dislike it may form a lasting negative association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand your brand across genres by identifying umbrella themes
rubrics_metrics.description: If you write in multiple genres, define broader, transferable elements (umbrella themes) that let a single brand cover diverse works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: translate 'magic system' into 'rule-based speculative elements' that apply to fantasy, sci‑fi, and detective fiction; Mary Robinette reframes her brand to an approach that supports multiple genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create multiple related brandings or an umbrella to cover diverse projects
rubrics_metrics.description: You can maintain several connected brand angles (rather than only one narrow label) to accommodate different kinds of work without confusing readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brandon describes having a couple of brandings and an interconnected universe (Cosmere) to allow work across different genres while keeping recognizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch how people talk about your work in public to refine brand choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor reviews, panel placement, and reader comments to see which elements of your writing are consistently noticed and valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use those observed highlights to inform pitches and marketing; what people naturally emphasize is often your best branding material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify recurring elements across your work that can become marketable messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns in your books (e.g., characters obsessed with specialists, recurring themes) can be packaged as a selling point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan's example: all main characters obsessed with an expert — find that pattern and shape it into a concise marketing message.
